The morning light hit the kitchen counter at a different angle today, and I noticed the scratch near the sink that I'd somehow missed for three years. It's strange what we become blind to, the way familiarity drapes itself over everything like a thin film, making the extraordinary ordinary and the ordinary invisible. I stood there with my coffee going cold, suddenly unable to remember if I'd put sugar in it or not, paralyzed by this tiny canyon in the laminate, wondering what else I'd failed to see.

My grandmother kept a drawer of batteries that never worked. Dead AAs, corroded 9-volts, all mixed together with twist ties and rubber bands and a single dice from a lost Monopoly set. Every time I visited, she'd ask me to test them, and I'd pretend, pressing the dead cylinders to my tongue to feel the faint chemical sting of the ones that still held some ghost of charge. She knew I was lying, I think. She kept asking anyway. The ritual mattered more than the result.

I've been thinking about rituals lately. The way I always put my left shoe on first. The specific number of stirs I give my tea—seven clockwise, one counterclockwise, superstition without belief. We are creatures of pattern, hungry for meaning in repetition, and maybe that's not so different from love, or prayer, or the way waves keep arriving at a shore that never thanks them.

Last Tuesday I found a dead moth in the pages of a library book. It left a powder stain on the paragraph where someone had underlined *"the heart has reasons that reason knows nothing of."* I stared at that moth for a long time, this creature that had spent its brief hours of flight seeking light, ending its life in the dark between borrowed pages, leaving only dust and a coincidental proximity to someone else's longing. I didn't know what to do with the body. I closed the book and returned it. Someone else will find it, or they won't. The library has its own rituals.

The scratch on the counter, I realized, probably came from the knife I use to cut limes. I drink a lot of lime water now, ever since I read somewhere that it helps with something—energy, digestion, the general sense of wrongness that accumulates in a body over time. I don't know if it works. I don't know if anything works, really, except the doing of it, the small daily motion toward some imagined better self who wakes up without that heaviness behind the eyes.

My neighbor practices piano at 6 AM. Chopin, mostly, halting and wrong-noted, the same measures repeated until they surrender. I used to resent the intrusion, the stolen sleep. Now I lie awake and listen for the moment when the repetition becomes music, when the struggle transforms into something that sounds like intention. It doesn't always happen. Some mornings she gives up and I hear the bench scrape back, the silence that follows somehow heavier than the mistakes. But when it clicks—when the nocturne actually nocturnes, when the melody lifts and carries—I feel something loosen in my chest, this vicarious triumph, proof that persistence can alchemize into grace.

I want to tell her I hear her. I never will. The anonymity is part of the gift, the way we can matter to strangers without knowing, the way that dead moth mattered to me, the way I maybe matter to someone I'll never meet, a presence in their periphery, a story they tell without my name.

The coffee was cold. I hadn't put sugar in it. I drank it anyway, standing at the sink, running my thumb across the scratch like reading braille, trying to learn what it had to teach me about attention, about time, about the slow erosion of surfaces that continues whether we witness it or not.

There are 983 words left, and I feel the pressure of them now, this arbitrary abundance, the way constraint creates its own freedom. I could tell you about the dream I had where I could only speak in questions, and everyone answered me with statements, and we couldn't understand each other at all. I could describe the particular shade of gray the sky turned yesterday before the rain, a color that doesn't have a name in any language I know, something between resignation and relief. I could list the contents of my pockets: a receipt for gas I don't remember buying, a guitar pick I found on the sidewalk and kept for luck, a folded note with a phone number I never called because the moment of finding it felt more significant than whatever conversation might follow.

Instead I'll tell you about the time I watched a man repair a watch in a shop window in Prague. He had a loupe screwed into his eye socket like a monocle from another century, and his hands moved with such deliberate slowness that I couldn't tell if he was working or praying. I stood there for forty minutes. Tourists flowed around me. The man never looked up. I don't know if he fixed the watch or not, but I carry that image with me, this figure of absolute concentration, this argument for patience in a world that keeps speeding toward destinations that dissolve on arrival.

We're down to 700 now, and I'm aware of the counting, the way the number itself becomes a presence in the room, a third party to this conversation, ticking down. I want to make them matter, these remaining words, but I also know that pressure is the enemy of whatever this is, this flow, this attempt to let something emerge without forcing shape upon it.

My mother called last week. We talked about the weather, her garden, whether I was eating enough vegetables. We didn't mention the thing we don't mention, the silence that sits between us like a piece of furniture we've both learned to navigate around. I love her in the way you love something that hurts to touch, the way you love a memory that keeps revising itself, the way you love a place you can never return to because it exists in time, not space, and time only moves one direction, relentless, indifferent, beautiful in its cruelty.

I keep a list of birds I've seen. Not a serious birder's list, nothing with dates or locations, just names accumulated over years of accidental attention: cardinal, blue jay, that one time a pileated woodpecker in the woods behind my uncle's house, the heron that stood in the retention pond like a question mark, the sparrows that are everywhere and therefore invisible until you force yourself to see them, their subtle variations, their persistent brown resilience. The list is in my phone, mixed with grocery reminders and half-written poems. Sometimes I scroll through it and try to remember the specific moment each name was added, the context of the seeing, what I was avoiding or seeking when I looked up and there was a bird, being a bird, unconcerned with my list, my need to catalog, my hunger for significance.

500 left. The halfway point, though "halfway" implies a destination, and I don't know where this is going, if anywhere. Maybe that's the point. Maybe the point is the opposite of a point, the spreading out, the refusal to arrive. I think about the ocean again, those waves, how each one is different and each one is the same, how the water doesn't care about our metaphors, how it just moves, moved by forces we can measure but not feel directly, the moon's invisible hand, the earth's turning, the wind's arbitrary urgencies.

I met a woman once who collected sand. Jars and jars from different beaches, labeled with dates, some with coordinates. She had sand from Antarctica, from the Sahara, from the artificial beach at a resort in Dubai. She told me each sample was a different color if you looked closely, that "sand" was a category like "bird" or "love," containing multitudes we collapse into single words for convenience. I wanted to ask her what she was looking for, if she ever found it, if the collection was about memory or aspiration or some attempt to hold the unholdable. I didn't ask. I bought her a drink and we talked about other things, the way you do, the way we protect each other from our own depths, our collections, our scratches and dead batteries and moths and sand.

I used to write letters. Actual letters, on paper, with stamps. There's one I never sent, still in a drawer, addressed to someone who wouldn't remember my name now, full of feeling I can no longer fully access, the self who wrote it foreign and familiar in equal measure. I keep it as evidence, I think, proof that I was capable of that articulation, that urgency, that willingness to risk exposure. The person I am now is more careful, more cold, more likely to put sugar in my coffee and not notice whether I did or not. I'm not sure if that's growth or damage, if the distinction matters, if anything matters in the way we want it to, the way we need it to, to keep moving through days that accumulate without necessarily adding up.

300 words. I can feel the end approaching, the way you feel a dream beginning to fray at the edges, the real world leaking in, the alarm clock or the light or the need to pee, some bodily insistence that interrupts the flight. I don't want to land yet. I want to keep circling, keep saying things that might matter to someone, might matter to me later when I reread this and wonder who wrote it, what they were feeling, what they were trying to avoid or approach.

The piano starts again. It's not Chopin this time, something I don't recognize, maybe original, maybe just unfamiliar. The mistakes are more frequent. The pauses longer. But there's a moment, right there, where something almost happens, a phrase that hangs in the air like a question, and I find myself holding my breath, waiting, hoping, this ridiculous hope, this persistent human capacity for investment in outcomes we can't control, in beauty that might not arrive, in love that might not be returned, in meaning that might not exist except in the making of it, the reaching toward, the wave after wave of attempt.

I want to be the moth and the reader who finds it. I want to be the piano and the neighbor who hears. I want to be the scratch and the thumb that reads it, the sand and the collector, the dead battery and the tongue that tests it, the letter and the sender and the one who never opens it, all of it, all at once, the fullness of being that we never quite achieve, the scattered pieces that never quite cohere, the story that continues after the last word, into silence, into the space where you are now, reading this, bringing your own scratches and rituals, your own morning light falling at whatever angle it falls where you are, making visible what was hidden, hiding what will become visible in time, in time, in the time we have left, which is always less than we think and always, somehow, exactly enough.

The coffee is gone. The counter is scratched. The words are almost spent. I don't know how to end this, so I won't, not really, I'll just stop, here, now, with this breath, this pause, this space for you to fill with whatever comes to you, whatever has been waiting, whatever needs the permission of an ending to begin.
